title: Should your clothing logo be embroidered or screen printed?
seoTitle: Embroidery or Screen Printing for a Clothing Logo?
description: Compare the same mark in thread and ink on the intended fabric. Check small lettering, weight, the reverse side and appearance after care.
author: BEWE4R team
intro: Choose embroidery when the stitched texture is part of the design and the fabric can support it comfortably. Consider screen printing when the artwork depends on a flat graphic surface or a larger area of colour. The most useful comparison is the same logo, at its actual size, on the intended garment fabric.

toc.text: Look at the smallest feature first
Ask for a trial that answers a production question
Can the same logo file be used for both embroidery and print?
Agree how to review it after care

bodyHtml:
Look at the smallest feature first

Imagine a wordmark with a small open space in the letter “e”. On screen it looks generous. At the size of a chest logo, thread may close that gap. Ink can also lose detail if the artwork and process are mismatched. Give the decorator both the original vector file and a drawing at finished size. Ask to see a trial of the smallest lettering before approving the whole logo.

Compare what the wearer experiences

Design questionEmbroidery trialScreen-print trial
How does the front look?Inspect stitch direction, edge definition and puckering.Inspect line edges, colour coverage and alignment.
What happens when the fabric bends?Check how the stitched area moves against the base.Fold the printed area and examine how the surface feels.
What touches the skin?Examine the reverse, backing and loose ends.Check the feel of the print in the intended coverage and position.

A small chest mark on a substantial sweatshirt and a wide back graphic on a lightweight tee are different jobs. It can make sense to use embroidery for one and screen print for the other while keeping the same underlying brand artwork.

Ask for a trial that answers a production question

Use the final fabric shade for the trial if colour contrast matters. A light logo on a dark garment can look different from the same design on white. Mark the approved thread or ink reference and keep the physical trial. If the supplier changes the fabric finish later, ask whether the original trial still represents the garment.

Can the same logo file be used for both embroidery and print?

Give both specialists the same approved brand artwork, then ask which production file or changes their process requires. An embroidery programme defines stitch paths and may simplify small features. Approve the visible stitched result beside the printed result at the intended size, and keep each production file tied to its own approved reference.

Agree how to review it after care

Wash and dry the sample under the proposed care conditions. Examine small openings, edges, fabric distortion and the feel against the skin. Photograph the same area before and after, with the sample identifier visible. These observations relate to the sample and conditions tested.

Compare the two methods in BEWE4R’s finishing gallery. To discuss a logo trial, send the finished dimensions, artwork file, fabric and placement.
